pointers.sentence: Django was built in a newspaper's newsroom in Lawrence, Kansas, and open-sourced in the summer of 2005 (`docs/faq/general.txt`).
The branch removed constraints on how code had to be written that "were a consequence of decisions made in the early days of Django, prior to its open-source release" (`docs/releases/0.95.txt`).

After the merge, models stayed in the module that defined them, a model overrode `Model.save` and `Model.delete` in their place, as any class overrides a method, and custom table-level functions went on a new Manager API (`django/db/models/manager.py:BaseManager`).
`LazySettings.configure` allows it now (`django/conf/__init__.py:LazySettings.configure`).
A project that defines none gets a `"default"` on the dummy backend, which raises when used (`django/db/utils.py:ConnectionHandler.configure_settings`).

`Model._meta` dates from the days of the magic-removal, say the 1.8 notes, and became an official API only in 1.8 (`docs/releases/1.8.txt`; [The options: what a model keeps as `_meta`](../models/options.md)).
Its notes said that the next release would move newforms to django.forms (`docs/releases/0.96.txt`).
The helpers form_for_model and form_for_instance gave way to `ModelForm` (`docs/releases/1.0.txt`).

A model's admin options live outside it, on a `ModelAdmin` registered for the model with `AdminSite.register` (`django/contrib/admin/sites.py:AdminSite.register`; [Registering models: `AdminSite.register` and `ModelAdmin`](../admin/registration.md)).
1.2 replaced them with `DATABASES`, connections by alias with one named `"default"` (`docs/releases/1.2.txt`).
Both keep those signatures (`django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.get_db_prep_value`).
1.3 configured caches "in the same way", by alias in `CACHES` (`docs/releases/1.3.txt`).

`ConnectionHandler` and `CacheHandler` are now both subclasses of `BaseConnectionHandler` (`django/utils/connection.py:BaseConnectionHandler`; [Connections by alias: `DATABASES` and `ConnectionHandler`](../connections/aliases.md)).

What stands now is `atomic`, a block that commits or rolls back and nests as savepoints (`django/db/transaction.py:Atomic`; [Transactions: autocommit, `atomic` and savepoints](../connections/atomic.md)).
Since 1.1 each of a `TestCase`'s tests had run in a transaction rolled back after it (`docs/releases/1.1.txt`).

1.8 ran them inside two nested `atomic` blocks: one for the class, where `TestCase.setUpTestData` runs, and one for each test (`docs/releases/1.8.txt`, `django/test/testcases.py:TestCase._enter_atomics`; [A transaction around each test: `TestCase`](../testing/test-case.md)).

Each application's module and then each models module is imported as Django starts, by one deterministic process that the notes expect to make import loops easier to diagnose: `Apps.populate`, which `django.setup` calls (`docs/releases/1.7.txt`, `django/apps/registry.py:Apps.populate`; [Populating the app registry](../startup/populate.md)).

Every field must describe itself for those files through a new required method, `Field.deconstruct` (`docs/releases/1.7.txt`, `django/db/models/fields/__init__.py:Field.deconstruct`; [Migrations](../migrations.md)).

Inside migrate, syncdb survives: with --run-syncdb, `Command.sync_apps` creates the tables of applications without migrations (`django/core/management/commands/migrate.py:Command.sync_apps`; [The migrate command, showmigrations and sqlmigrate](../migrations/migrate.md)).

A comment does: to skip South's, `MigrationQuestioner.ask_initial` has makemigrations write no first migration for an application whose migrations package holds a Python file other than `"__init__.py"`, unless the command names it (`django/db/migrations/questioner.py:MigrationQuestioner.ask_initial`).

In 2014 DEP 1 set up a process for proposals, a near-copy of Python's PEP process (`deps:final/0001-dep-process.rst`; [Where Django came from, and who makes it](../introduction/origins.md#django-enhancement-proposals)).
1.1 had added aggregates, `QuerySet.aggregate` and `QuerySet.annotate`, and `F`, a reference to another field (`docs/releases/1.1.txt`).
Aggregates were not expressions at all, so two could not be added to each other; annotate took nothing but aggregates (`deps:final/0181-orm-expressions.rst`).

An `Aggregate` is a `Func` like any database function, and `F`, as the DEP proposed, is not an expression but resolves to one (`django/db/models/aggregates.py:Aggregate`, `django/db/models/expressions.py:F.resolve_expression`; [Expressions: `resolve_expression` and `as_sql`](../expressions/protocol.md)).

It proposed a stable API for template backends, with Jinja2 built in and the Django template language kept as the default (`deps:final/0182-multiple-template-engines.rst`).

`TEMPLATES` lists the engines, and `get_template` asks them in order until one finds the template (`django/template/loader.py:get_template`; [Template engines: `TEMPLATES` and the backends](../templates/engines.md)).

Since users would have to write `TEMPLATES` anyway, 1.8 also moved the context processors out of django.core, where the magic-removal had left them, to `django.template.context_processors` (`deps:final/0182-multiple-template-engines.rst`, `docs/releases/1.8.txt`).

Since users would have to write `TEMPLATES` anyway, 1.8 also moved the context processors out of django.core, where the magic-removal had left them, to `django.template.context_processors` (`deps:final/0182-multiple-template-engines.rst`, `docs/releases/1.8.txt`).

So `TEMPLATES` is a list, where `DATABASES` and `CACHES` are dictionaries: its order decides which engine wins, and a project can put replacements for an application's templates first (`deps:final/0182-multiple-template-engines.rst`).
